title: Lamar Jackson Returns to Practice; Ravens’ Game‑Time Status Still Uncertain vs. Bengals
body:
Baltimore’s star quarterback Lamar Jackson stepped onto the practice field Wednesday after missing the previous two games with a sore left ankle, but his participation in Sunday’s showdown with the Cincinnati Bengals remains far from certain. Though the two‑time NFL MVP completed a limited drill, observers noted a pronounced limp as he entered the Ravens’ training complex, underscoring lingering concerns about his mobility and durability.

Jackson’s injury, initially diagnosed as a high‑ankle sprain during the team’s week‑two loss to the Cleveland Browns, has kept him sidelined for a total of 13 snaps. The Ravens’ medical staff cleared him for “non‑contact” activity, allowing him to run a few plays in a controlled environment. However, the quarterback’s gait and the visible favoring of his left foot suggest that the ankle has not yet regained full stability. Head coach John Harbaugh, who has been tight‑lipped about the timeline for Jackson’s return, indicated that the decision will hinge on the player’s ability to execute a full range of motion without pain.

The stakes are high for Baltimore. After a 2‑1 start to the season, the Ravens sit at 3‑4 and are fighting to stay within striking distance of the AFC North’s playoff picture. A win over the Bengals—who have already secured a postseason berth—could provide a crucial boost to morale and momentum. Yet, the team must weigh the risk of aggravating Jackson’s ankle against the potential upside of his electrifying playmaking. In his absence, backup quarterback Tyler Huntley has managed the offense with modest success, guiding the unit to a 20‑13 victory over the Denver Broncos last week. Huntley’s poise has earned praise, but his limited mobility and lack of a dual‑threat skill set leave the Ravens’ offense less dynamic than when Jackson is at the helm.

Analysts are divided on whether Baltimore should gamble on Jackson’s return. Some argue that his presence alone forces defenses to respect the run‑pass option, opening up opportunities for the Ravens’ running backs and tight ends even if Jackson is limited. Others caution that a compromised ankle could hamper his signature scrambling ability, potentially leading to turnovers or further injury. “The quarterback’s health is the most valuable asset we have,” said former NFL scout Mike Gentry. “If he’s not 100 percent, the risk of a broken ankle is real, and that could sideline him for the rest of the season.”

The decision also carries implications for the broader AFC landscape. A victory would tighten the race for the division’s second wild‑card spot, pitting Baltimore against teams like the Los Angeles Chargers and the New England Patriots for the final postseason berth. Conversely, a loss could see the Ravens slip further behind, forcing them into a must‑win scenario for the remainder of the schedule. The Bengals, meanwhile, will likely exploit any hesitation from Baltimore’s coaching staff, knowing that a healthy Jackson can dramatically shift the tempo of a game.

As the clock ticks down to Sunday’s kickoff, the Ravens will convene a final assessment meeting with Jackson, the medical team, and senior coaches. The outcome will determine whether the franchise’s marquee player will take the field or remain on the sidelines while Huntley continues to steer the offense. Regardless of the decision, Baltimore’s path to the playoffs will hinge on its ability to adapt, manage injuries prudently, and capitalize on the opportunities that arise in a tightly contested AFC North. The upcoming showdown promises to be a defining moment for both Jackson’s health trajectory and the Ravens’ postseason aspirations.
